message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This review is grounded in two months of actual till data for every main course, a full competitor price check, and the latest supplier information, so the recommendations are not guesswork. The price increases are modest and targeted: each of the three dishes stays below the midpoint of competitor prices for that dish, so we remain the value option in the area, and with 60% of bookings from repeat guests our customer base is loyal enough to absorb a pound or two. The projected effect is simple to check, £810 a week or about £42,000 a year in additional gross profit, which lifts our main-course margin to about 71%. I also think the menu-mix decision is clear-cut: the data show the mushroom risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so replacing it with a seasonal special is an easy improvement. Monitoring for eight weeks gives us an early warning if volumes move. Overall I believe these changes are sensible, low-risk and well evidenced.
</author>

<document>
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.
</document>
response:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026 (The Copper Kettle)

The table arithmetic is correct, and so is the £810 sum. The competitor-midpoint claims also hold.

The two main conclusions don't hold:

- **The risotto has the highest margin on the menu, not the weakest.** Replacing it is likely to cost money.
- **The £42,000 projection leaves out the beef price rise.** The paper itself reports a 12% increase on 1 April, the same day the new prices start. It may also count VAT as profit.

Corrected for these, the price increases are still worth making. The likely gain is around half the stated figure, and the risotto swap could give back a large share of it.

## 1. The risotto decision is reversed by the paper's own table

Table 1's figures, recalculated:

| Dish | Margin % | Gross profit per plate | Plates/week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mushroom risotto | **80%** (highest) | £11.20 | 90 |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 | 180 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 | 260 |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 | 310 |
| Sirloin steak | 60% | £15.60 | 120 |
| Specials | 64% | — | 90 |

- **Margin.** The risotto has the highest percentage margin. Its cash profit per plate is also above the burger and the curry.
- **Sales.** It is tied for lowest with specials, not uniquely lowest.
- **The replacement.** It is a special "at the same price." Specials currently run at 64%. A £14 special at that margin earns £8.96 a plate against the risotto's £11.20, which loses about **£200 a week (around £10,500 a year)** on unchanged volume.

The case for removing the risotto, if there is one, has to rest on popularity or menu appeal, not margin. On margin, there is a case for featuring it more prominently.

## 2. The projection leaves out the beef increase

Section 4 reports that beef rises 12% from 1 April. Section 5.3 treats every extra pound of price as extra profit. The paper doesn't say what share of each plate cost is beef, so here is the range:

- **Upper bound, if the whole plate cost were beef:**
  - steak: £1.25 more per plate, £150 a week;
  - burger: £0.50 more per plate, £131 a week;
  - total: **£281 a week**.
- **Plausible estimate**, with steak mostly beef and the burger patty about half its cost: **around £190–£200 a week**.

On the steak, most of the £2 rise goes on the new beef cost. On the burger, much of the £1 rise does.

The margin claim changes too. Including specials at an assumed £16, main-course margin is now about 69%. The price rises alone would lift it to about 71%, as the paper says. With the beef increase it ends nearer **70%**, or about 69% at the upper bound.

## 3. Check whether the figures include VAT

UK menu prices include VAT, at 20% on restaurant food. Table 1 calculates margins on menu prices, and the £810 is gross of VAT. If so:

- Only £675 of the £810 a week is actual extra revenue.
- The margins in Table 1 are not on the same basis as the accounts' 67–70% food margin, assuming the accounts are prepared ex-VAT.

Confirm which basis the 67% and 70% figures use before comparing them with Table 1.

## 4. Corrected projection

| | Per week | Per year |
|---|---|---|
| As stated | £810 | £42,120 |
| Less likely beef cost increase | about −£195 | |
| Ex-VAT (if prices include VAT) | about −£135 | |
| **Price increases, corrected** | **about £480** | **about £25,000** |
| Risotto swap at specials margin | about −£200 | about −£10,500 |
| **Both proposals together** | **about £280** | **about £14,500** |

These figures still assume volumes hold, and every other figure depends on that assumption.

## 5. "Volumes will hold" needs testing, not asserting

- **Loyal guests still notice prices.** The 60% repeat figure means most guests will notice the rises, since they know the old prices. Loyalty may well absorb a pound, but the paper doesn't show it.
- **No longer the cheapest.** After the rises, all three dishes are above the cheapest competitor: £17.50 against £16.95, £16.00 against £15.50, and £28 against £27. "Below the midpoint" holds, but "lowest in the group" no longer does. The positioning change deserves to be stated openly.
- **The 2024 precedent.** "No visible effect on bookings" doesn't give the size of that rise, and bookings are not main-course volumes.
- **Weekday lunch.** "A small share" is unsupported. Friday and Saturday dinner are just under half of mains, so the other eight services, including five lunches, are just over half.
- **Sensitivity.** A break-even line would help: how far can volume fall before the rise loses money, compared with leaving prices unchanged while beef costs rise anyway? With the corrections above, the margin for error is smaller than the paper implies.

## 6. The monitoring baseline will mislead

Comparing April and May with January and February confounds the price effect with seasonality. January and February are usually the quietest months, so volumes will likely rise in spring whatever the prices. That could hide a real loss of trade. Two better comparisons:

- the same weeks of 2025;
- the mix share of each dish, which seasonality affects less than raw volumes.

Also state in advance what result would trigger a rethink.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Trading days.** Section 8 says "six trading days a week," but Section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five.
- **Where the margin slipped.** On Table 1, main courses are already at about 69–70%, so the slide to 67% overall must come mostly from other courses. The paper raises only main-course prices without showing where the margin fell.
- **Annualising.** "×52" assumes no closure weeks.
- **Fish cost risk.** Fish and chips is the largest contributor to the gain, and Section 4 calls fish prices volatile.
- **Scope of the competitor check.** It covered only three dishes. The curry (75% margin, unchanged price) and the risotto weren't checked, and there may be room on the curry.
- **Not drawing attention to the increases.** This is legitimate, but with a 60% repeat base it carries a trust risk if guests feel the change was slipped past them.

## Recommendation

- **Approve the price increases**, restating the expected gain as about £20,000–£25,000 a year, net of beef costs and VAT.
- **Do not remove the risotto on margin grounds.** If the menu needs a seasonal change, cost the replacement special to at least the risotto's £11.20 profit per plate.
- **Before 1 April:** confirm the VAT basis of the margin figures, get the beef share of the burger and steak costs, and set a year-on-year monitoring baseline with a stated trigger.
